Humanitarian finance Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email GENEVA Norwegian People’s Aid will turn down millions in US government funding due to wide-reaching restrictions on reproductive health and equity, the mine action group announced, in a rare example of a humanitarian organisation publicly rejecting US cash. The decision could affect 40% of NPA’s de-mining budget and 1,700 jobs, and will have “major consequences” for the organisation, NPA said. Few humanitarian groups have spoken publicly about the so-called “global gag rules” since the Trump administration expanded the discriminatory restrictions this year . The regulations, known as the Mexico City policy, handcuff organisations receiving US cash even if potentially banned work is paid for in separate budgets by other donors. Over decades, the US has repeatedly rescinded then reinstated the global gag rule as the government lurches between Democrat and Republican-led administrations. “I think it’s an important time to stand up for the rights that we’ve been fighting for – the system that we’ve been fighting for – for so many years.” Previous versions have tried to block organisations that receive US health funding from providing or promoting abortion care as part of family planning – even if the money came from other sources. This year, the Trump administration has expanded the rules to cover almost all foreign aid including humanitarian funding, and to target gender identity and diversity, equity, and inclusion. “We see that a more rights-based approach is being challenged globally,” Gry Ballestad, NPA’s director of policy and communications, said in an interview. “And I think it’s an important time to stand up for the rights that we’ve been fighting for – the system that we’ve been fighting for – for so many years.” The restrictions affecting NPA cover funding from the US State Department’s Office of Weapons Removal and Abatement. Critics say the global gag rules are an attempt to co-opt international aid along US ideological lines. The US made drastic cuts to humanitarian budgets when it dismantled its aid programme last year, which could lead to millions of deaths, a study published in The Lancet estimated. But other governments are also cutting back – leaving the US as a top humanitarian donor that can shape how and where the system works by sheer volume. For example, the US has earmarked some $3.75 billion to UN-run pooled funds – roughly 83% of total funds so far, and $3.6 billion more than the next largest donor. It has also promised hundreds of millions more directly to UN agencies like the World Food Programme and UNICEF, or non-governmental organisations like World Vision . The initial $2 billion to UN pooled funds was signed just before the global gag rule’s new restrictions came into effect. Ballestad spoke to The New Humanitarian about NPA’s decision, its consequences, and what this moment means for the wider humanitarian and development sectors. This interview was edited for length and clarity. The New Humanitarian: Can you describe the decision-making process: What were the considerations? Gry Ballestad: It’s been a difficult decision given the implications, the programmes it affects around the world, the size of the funding, all the people that will be losing their jobs, and the impact on the ground. It’s been a very difficult decision to take. In [2026], the big change for us was that now the requirements are not just for the American funding – not just the mine action programmes funded by the State Department, but it would affect also all our other activities and programmes... This would put limitations on everything we do – not just the American funding. When we started working with the Americans, these were not the requirements we signed on to – actually, quite the opposite. For a long time, it’s been a requirement that we do take into consideration equal opportunities and all these things that are now a problem. We see that now, with the change in the requirements, and looking at our core values and principles, that it’s such a big change that we cannot accept it. Because there’s a change in the regulation, we would basically have to change our core values, our activities – really, who we are. NPA is not just working on mine action. We are the humanitarian solidarity organisation of the labour movement. That’s our origin. Our core values are very much linked to the labour movement. They’re very close to us still. Basically, we would have to change who we are. We would have to change our core values. We have a big programme in Norway that’s working on search-and-rescue activities, but also integration activities. For example, today we had the launch of our new anti-racism guidelines for our members, and other organisations, on how to work on anti-racism. We have local chapters all over the country, and they are very much involved in integration and anti-racism activities. We couldn’t do that. It would affect what we do also in Norway together with our partners around the world. And it’s not something we can accept. It’s beyond the American funding. It would affect who we are, how we operate. Of course, we can’t change our identity and all of our activities because one of our donors changed their requirements. The New Humanitarian: I think what people might not understand is how far the global gag rule reaches. Ballestad: It’s very broad. For us, it’s very much about who we are. What are the core values of an organisation like NPA? The first paragraph of our principles ... says “Norwegian People’s Aid’s values are based on equal rights for all regardless of gender, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, functional ability, and social status. Norwegian People's Aid is an anti-racist organisation.” That’s the first paragraph. So already there, we’re in trouble. What’s the game-changer this time: The [US] requirements that came out in [2025] were similar, but they were only for American-funded activities. This time, it would cover all of what we do. You can’t compensate for what you can’t do with American funding with other funding. It would affect who we are, how we operate. Of course, we can’t change our identity and all of our activities because one of our donors changed their requirements. It’s basically about our political freedom. The New Humanitarian: Many mine action programmes have focused on recruiting women as de-miners. Is something like that – the US would consider that to be non-compliant? Ballestad: Yes. When we advertise, for example, sometimes we encourage women to apply so that we can have more of a gender balance in, for example, our management positions. This, we wouldn’t be allowed to do. And we do that for everything. That’s part of our HR policies. There’s a lot of levels that we would have to change. We can’t accept it. Of course, Americans set their requirements for their funding. But we have to assess if this is something we can accept to remain true to our foundational values. The New Humanitarian: Looking at the entire aid sector, why do you think it’s important that NPA made this decision? What’s the significance of it? Ballestad: In the bigger picture, we see that a more rights-based approach is being challenged globally. And I think it’s an important time to stand up for the rights that we’ve been fighting for – the system that we’ve been fighting for – for so many years. It costs, if you stand up for rights. And I think it’s the time to do so. It’s a slippery slope... Currently, these are the rights we’re discussing. You don’t know what’s next. When do you put your foot down? Edited by Andrew Gully. https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/analy.body: Home West Africa Nigeria Related stories Conflict Opinion 11 September 2026 Visible crises, invisible people Conflict News 7 September 2026 EXCLUSIVE: Nigerian government and Boko Haram strike secret ceasefire deal Conflict Feature 3 September 2026 Lives on hold: Young Iranians watch their futures slip away Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email Editor's note: This is the second article in a series exploring the feasibility of dialogue as a path to peace in Africa’s protracted civil conflicts. Read the first report here . MAIDUGURI, Nigeria Mamman Nur, the senior cleric of Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), had tried to escape detention by his own comrades twice before – he knew this failed third attempt was likely his death sentence. The influential ideologue had been a leading figure in Nigeria’s insurgent jihadist movement for more than two decades. He had been one of the closest aides to Boko Haram’s deceased founder, Mohammed Yusuf, was a key link to Islamic State-Central, and for a time was popularly thought of as ISWAP’s leader. But the tall, charismatic teacher was now undone. He had been accused of secret contact with the Nigerian government through an initiative known as the “Swiss process”, which was exploring a path to dialogue and regarded Nur as a possible interlocutor . To ISWAP’s governing Shura council, this was treason. With the blessing of IS-Central, Nur was detained while the council debated what to do. In September 2018, he was sentenced to death and publicly shot by the head of the amniya , ISWAP’s secret police. Nur’s fate exposed the central problem facing any attempt to negotiate with Nigeria’s jihadists: Can a movement that treats dialogue as treason ever be persuaded to make peace? Nearly eight years later, a reported ceasefire between the government and Boko Haram suggests that, however tentatively, the answer may be changing. Can you make peace with jihadists? After 17 years of war and close to 350,000 indirect civilian deaths , the conflict in Nigeria’s northeast is stalemated. Yet behind the scenes there has been a long if faltering attempt by the Nigerian government to find a negotiated breakthrough to the jihadist insurgency. The idea of negotiations with “Boko Haram” – officially Jama’at Ahl al Sunna li Da’wa wal Jihad (JAS) – and ISWAP, its offshoot and rival, sharply divides Nigeria. The government officially says there can be no talks with groups legally proscribed as terrorist organisations, even though a three-month ceasefire with JAS, agreed in June, seems to be holding . The New Humanitarian has spoken to security officials, diplomats, mediators, and former jihadist fighters – protecting their anonymity so they could speak freely – to explore the potential of that dialogue process. Is there a path to a sustainable peace with extremist groups that reject the legitimacy of the Nigerian state, its secular constitution, and world view? “Both sides believe a settlement is possible,” a diplomat with knowledge of the chronology of the dialogue process told The New Humanitarian. “For all parties, a non-kinetic [military] approach is intellectually acceptable.” Military operations alone rarely resolves insurgencies. Political settlements, where they are possible, are more likely to produce lasting peace. But governments tend to exceptionalise jihadist groups and publicly shun the idea of dialogue with people typically characterised as irredeemably violent. These groups’ perceived maximalist ideological demands are seen as obstacles to peace – the spiritual and sacred regarded as incompatible with the give and take of political bargaining. Yet Islamist ideology is not monolithic . Extremist groups are political actors that shape and are shaped by their environments. Supposed “red lines” over political demands can also fade over time. In Egypt, Gama’a al Islamiya carried out armed attacks for two decades before it renounced violence and stood in elections in 2011. And more recently, in Syria, Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham transformed from an al-Qaeda franchise into the dominant force behind a transitional government. However, the cell-like structures of jihadist groups, legal prohibitions, histories of distrust, and the difficulty of building domestic political consensus all weigh on the timing and incentives for peace talks. Negotiations demand patience, political will, and good intelligence networks, said the diplomat. Nigeria has struggled on all three fronts. Successive governments have also avoided confronting the grievances driving the northeastern conflict or properly understanding their opponents. The traditional establishment approach has been to “settle” troublemakers, buying them off with money and positions. But JAS and ISWAP have been different: ideological foes not seeking a financial reward or patronage. “Peace can be possible, but it needs trust and sincerity,” a former ISWAP commander who surrendered to the authorities last year, told The New Humanitarian. “The problem is that up until now, nobody has sat with [JAS/ISWAP] to understand them. A close observer of the Nigerian conflict was more sceptical. “The record shows that jihadist groups, like other insurgent groups, can engage in negotiations, at least preliminary or limited ones, when they are under pressure,” he noted. However, there are fewer examples of longer-term political solutions. Talking about talks The insurgency, which began in northeastern Maiduguri in 2009, was still growing when President Goodluck Jonathan was elected two years later. A southern Christian, his poll victory sparked riots in several predominantly Muslim northern cities in a controversy over whether he should have stood. For some in his administration it was proof of a conspiracy : that JAS was manufactured by aggrieved northern elites to undermine Jonathan’s rule. In the early days of the conflict, mediation efforts were largely privately led. Former president Olusegun Obasanjo made the first attempt in 2011, followed by Sheikh Ibrahim Datti Ahmad, the respected president of the National Supreme Council of Sharia. Both ended almost as soon as they had begun – with each side blaming the other. Demands by JAS were basic: the release of detained wives and colleagues, the rebuilding of homes and buildings destroyed by the security forces in Maiduguri, the payment of compensation to families of members killed, and the prosecution of the policemen responsible for the assassination of Yusuf, the movement’s founder. They have not included larger ideological goals. Splits and rivalries: A timeline of Boko Haram/ISWAP discord Boko Haram began as an ultra-conservative religious movement in the early 2000s in Maiduguri under a young cleric, Mohammed Yusuf. It tapped into a radical zeitgeist that appealed across classes – condemning so-called “Western values” and celebrating 500 years of Islamic learning and empire in Nigeria’s northeast. Initially, Yusuf resisted calling for jihad, but as tensions with the authorities increased, he launched an urban insurrection in July 2009. It was quickly crushed, and Yusuf was extrajudicially killed by the police. Abubakar Shekau, his deputy, took over as imam. A wave of bombings, kidnappings, and the overrunning of towns had the army on the backfoot, and rural Borno emptied as people were displaced from their homes. Shekau declared allegiance to so-called Islamic State in 2015 and the group was renamed Islamic State of West Africa Province (ISWAP). In 2016, ISWAP split. Dissident commanders led by Abu Musa al-Barnawi and cleric Mamman Nur accused Shekau of despotism and condemned his use of “takfir” – the death penalty for infidels – against rural civilians. Bitter factional fighting followed, but the dissidents managed to establish themselves in the Lake Chad region and win the blessing of IS-Central. Shekau reverted to his group’s previous Boko Haram desi

https://astana.osce.org/news/programme-o.body: News News Item OSCE supports evidence-based basin planning through stakeholder consultations and data verification in Kazakhstan Issued on: 4 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Astana From 26 July to 4 August 2026, the OSCE Programme Office in Astana, in partnership with the Information and Analytical Center for Water Resources under the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation, supported a series of consultations with basin inspections and other water-sector stakeholders in the Aral-Syrdarya, Zhaiyk-Caspian and Yertis basins. The consultations formed part of Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to develop basin plans and a General Plan for integrated water resources management based on accurate, up-to-date and jointly verified data. The consultations brought together more than 100 representatives of basin inspections, branches of the Republican State Enterprise (RSE) “Kazvodkhoz” and RSE “Kazhydromet”, local executive bodies, water-user organizations, and scientific and research institutions. Conducted by a team of three water specialists (two women and one man), the meetings took place from 26 to 29 July in Kyzylorda, from 30 to 31 July in Aktau, and from 2 to 4 August in Semey and Oskemen. Participants worked to verify baseline data, align projected water balances with local investment and development plans, and identify measures for inclusion in the basin plans. The consultations combined technical review with field observation. Participants examined water-use limits, the accuracy of water accounting and metering, the condition of hydraulic infrastructure and irrigation canals, transportation losses, and the fulfilment of transboundary commitments. Discussions also addressed the functioning of basin councils, the participation of water users and the public, and the availability and quality of data required for basin planning. Field visits to key water infrastructure and water-use facilities enabled participants to connect the planning process with conditions on the ground. Working directly with the expert team, representatives of the basin inspections also reconciled discrepancies between primary reporting data and previously prepared analytical materials. This included correcting data on water-supply sources and transboundary inflows in the three basins, strengthening the basis for calculating water balances under current and future demand scenarios. The consultations also highlighted priorities for continued investment in canal rehabilitation, water-saving technologies and monitoring networks. By bringing together national authorities, basin inspections, water users and other stakeholders to verify data and jointly identify priorities, the consultations strengthened the evidentiary basis for Kazakhstan’s basin plans and General Plan for integrated water resources management. The initiative supports the country’s long-term efforts to strengthen water security, transboundary co-operation and sustainable water governance, in line with OSCE commitments and international good practices. https://tntd.osce.org/news/transnational.body: PROTECT: Project on the Protection of Vulnerable Targets from Terrorist Attacks Project Update OSCE expands access to its technical guidance on the physical security of critical infrastructure: Release of official Turkmen version Issued on: 30 June 2026 Issued by: Transnational Threats Department , OSCE Centre in Ashgabat Fields of work: Countering terrorism On 29 and 30 June, the OSCE Centre in Ashgabat and the OSCE Transnational Threats Department launched the Turkmen version of their Technical Guide on Physical Security Considerations for Protecting Critical Infrastructure from Terrorist Attacks . The launch event was accompanied by a training course on enhancing the physical security of critical infrastructure from terrorist attacks, using the Technical Guide as a training aid. Developed under the OSCE’s Project PROTECT with support from Germany and the United States of America, the Technical Guide provides practical guidance to policymakers, critical infrastructure owners and operators, and security practitioners on enhancing the protection of critical infrastructure sites from terrorist attacks. The publication consolidates publicly available practices and examples from across the OSCE area and is designed to support stakeholders in developing security measures tailored to their specific risk environment. It was released in November 2025 in the English and Russian. The launch of the Turkmen language version of this Guide, initiated by the OSCE Centre in Ashgabat, is a testament to the Guide's growing value in OSCE participating States. A representative of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Turkmenistan presented the country's approach to protecting critical infrastructure, highlighting current practices, the national legislative framework and ongoing efforts to strengthen the security and resilience of critical infrastructure. The training course brought together government officials responsible for critical infrastructure protection to strengthen their understanding of physical security principles and practices. Participants examined approaches to security system design as well as technical measures including perimeter protection, intrusion detection systems, security lighting, video surveillance, access control and security screening. During the event, participants explored practical ways to apply the Guide’s principles through security assessments, emergency planning, business continuity measures and training exercises. “The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe serves as a vital pillar in global counter-terrorism efforts by actively strengthening the resilience and protection of critical infrastructure across its 57 participating States. Bearing in mind that security is not a task for a single agency or nation, we designed this training programme to build our collective resilience. It is our firm belief that this programme, together with the Guide, will strengthen inter-agency communication and help upgrade security protocols to more effectively protect critical infrastructure from terrorist attacks,” said William Leaf, Head of the OSCE Centre in Ashgabat. The event featured contributions from international experts and practitioners, as well as the Government of Kazakhstan, another key stakeholder in the OSCE’s Project PROTECT. A representative of the Anti-Terrorism Centre of the Committee of National Security of the Republic of Kazakhstan delivered a presentation on the country's approach to protecting critical infrastructure from terrorist threats. The event forms part of the OSCE Centre in Ashgabat's project Building Capacity of Law Enforcement and Security Officials of Turkmenistan in Countering Transnational Threats Related to Organized Crime and Terrorism – 2026 and the OSCE's extrabudgetary Project PROTECT, which supports participating States in strengthening national approaches to protecting vulnerable targets from terrorist threats and other hazards. More information on Project PROTECT can be found here . The Technical Guide on Physical Security Considerations for Protecting Critical Infrastructure from Terrorist Attacks can be found here . https://bih.osce.org/news/mission-bosnia.body: News News Item Public broadcasters must not amplify the glorification of convicted war criminals Issued on: 7 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina , OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media Fields of work: Human rights , Rule of law SARAJEVO/VIENNA, 07 September 2026 - The OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina and the OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media express serious concern regarding RTRS’s direct live transmission of a commemoration at which speakers repeatedly glorified Ratko Mladić. His convictions for genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war were upheld on appeal in 2021, as was his sentence of life imprisonment. Reporting on events of legitimate public interest is an essential part of media freedom and editorial independence. While reporting on events of public interest falls within the media’s editorial remit, particular concern arises given that content glorifying a convicted war criminal was amplified without adequate editorial context or reference to judicially established facts. Public service broadcasters have a particular responsibility to provide accurate, impartial and properly contextualized journalism. The Mission recalls that Article 145a(6) of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina criminalizes the glorification of persons sentenced by final judgment for such crimes. Whether the broadcast may have breached criminal law is for the competent justice institutions to determine. Separately, the Mission and the Representative call on the Communications Regulatory Agency to assess the coverage promptly and independently, including under Articles 4(8), 5 and 7 of the CRA Code on Programme Content, and to respond proportionately to any violation established. Respect for judicially established facts and for the dignity of victims and survivors is fundamental to responsible journalism, reconciliation and lasting peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Any media coverage of the forthcoming funeral should accordingly be accurate, properly contextualized and consistent with applicable professional and ethical standards. https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/opini.body: Home Asia Nepal Related stories Environment and Disasters Analysis 1 September 2026 The Himalayan disaster Nepal could not see coming Environment and Disasters Investigations 2 December 2021 How Bangladesh is beating the odds on climate disaster deaths Share & more Republish article Share Share on Bluesky Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share via WhatsApp Share via email DAKAR Rajendra Dawadi had to make a decision in an instant. Warned that floodwaters were racing towards his school in Nepal’s Trishuli Valley, the headmaster had no way of knowing how much time he had, nor whether the floodwaters would reach his school. He did not hesitate and evacuated more than 900 students and 16 staff to higher ground. Approximately 13 minutes later, a wall of water, mud, and debris swept through the area, destroying the school. Dawadi acted before he knew for certain what was coming. His calculation was simple. If the warning proved wrong, his students would miss a day of school . If it was right and he did nothing, hundreds of children could die. The instinct to act while there is still time, despite uncertainty, is at the heart of anticipatory action. Investing ahead of known risks has been shown to save lives and reduce losses . But acting ahead requires accepting that some forecasts will never provide complete certainty, and that waiting to act can carry far higher consequences. Nepal shows what formal systems can and cannot do Nepal is hardly a newcomer to acting ahead of disasters. The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology introduced the flood early warning system in the 1990s, combining both high-tech river level monitoring stations with simpler community-based systems for detecting rising waters and disseminating warnings. In 2022, the government held the first national dialogue on anticipatory action, and this year endorsed a national policy. Humanitarian organisations have been experimenting with anticipatory approaches for more than a decade , releasing pre-arranged emergency funding at least twice for flood response. The August disaster , however, fell outside of the mainly weather-related monsoon flooding that these mechanisms were designed to anticipate and warn against. A huge section of glacier and surrounding bedrock collapsed high in Tibet , sending ice, rock, and debris into the river system and generating a catastrophic flood that travelled nearly 100 kilometres downstream. Automatic monitoring stations along the upper Bhotekoshi River were meant to detect rising water and alert communities downstream, but the flood moved so quickly that monitoring stations inside Nepal were destroyed before they could transmit a warning. The community-level river gauges that gradually measured river behaviour were also too slow for a flood travelling at an average speed of 193 kilometres per hour . Some of these limitations were already understood. A 2023 review of Nepal’s anticipatory action experience raised concerns about the reliability of forecasts and called for greater flexibility to combine scientific triggers with human judgement and changing conditions on the ground. A later study in 2025 found their early warning messaging system frequently did not prompt the necessary actions to save lives and protect assets. What happened at Dawadi’s school shows why this matters. The warning that saved Dawadi’s students did not come through the formal monitoring or early warning system. A relative upstream called the school accountant. Teachers received calls from family and friends. A parent arrived to collect her child. Dawadi ordered the evacuation. Teachers, parents, and others then helped get the children uphill. Many others were not so fortunate. Elsewhere along the flood’s path, people had almost no time to react . Forecasting and early warning technology remain essential, but they have to be matched by readiness at the community level – evacuation plans, trusted communication networks, prepared local institutions and people able to act when information arrives. Those community connections are part of the infrastructure of disaster readiness. I saw their importance when I lived in Japan and studied how the country prepares for disasters in 2019. Japan is famous for its enormous investment in seawalls, flood defences, earthquake-resistant buildings and sophisticated warning systems. But some of its most important investments are far simpler . Children learn about disaster risk from kindergarten. Communities practise evacuations. Families are encouraged to have a go-bag ready at all times. Residents identify neighbours who may need help. Survivors share their experiences with communities facing similar hazards. Japan also shows the limits of relying too heavily on infrastructure and more formal warning systems. During severe 2018 flooding in Mabi , a district in western Japan situated near two rivers, embankments were overwhelmed and mobile-phone warnings failed to reach some of the elderly people most at risk. Research after the Mabi flood and the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake and Tsunami found that some residents delayed evacuating because they believed physical defences would protect them . Forecasting and early warning technology remain essential, but they have to be matched by readiness at the community level – evacuation plans, trusted communication networks, prepared local institutions and people able to act when information arrives. These investments may be less visible than satellites, monitoring stations or dams, but they can determine whether a warning actually saves a life. Schools are an important part of that community readiness. My research on education and anticipatory action with the Geneva Global Hub for Education in Emergencies in 2025 * found much the same thing that Dawadi’s experience demonstrates: Schools can play a critical role in turning early warnings into action. They reach children and families every day, while teachers are often trusted community leaders who can communicate risks, organise evacuations, and connect formal warning systems with local knowledge. Disaster education also gives children knowledge they take home and carry into adulthood, strengthening the ability of entire communities to respond to future crises. Governments, donors, and aid agencies must become more comfortable spending money before they can be certain a crisis will unfold as forecast. Scientists are still grappling with how to predict rock-ice avalanches like the one in Nepal. But as glacial flooding increases as a result of global warming , they warn that these events are expected to be more common around the world. Anticipatory approaches and funding will need to adapt to include these emerging risks while investing more in the local institutions and relationships that can turn warnings into action. Yet humanitarian financing still runs overwhelmingly in the opposite direction. Ninety-nine percent of international humanitarian funding still flows after disasters happen and only about 12% of total anticipatory action funding between 2022 and 2023 involved those organisations closest to communities. In a time of collapsing budgets and hyper-prioritisation, it is urgent to rethink whether scarce resources are being deployed where – and when – they can have the greatest effect. Some actions may prove unnecessary. Sometimes, supplies will be moved for a flood that changes course. Cash may be released ahead of a drought that proves less severe than expected. Schools may close for storms that never arrive. That does not make those decisions bad ones. Governments, donors, and aid agencies must become more comfortable spending money before they can be certain a crisis will unfold as forecast. The cost of acting unnecessarily can be far smaller than the cost of acting too late. Dawadi understood that tradeoff. *This article was revised on 10 September 2026 to show that the research was published in 2025, rather than 2024 as originally stated. Sha

https://odihr.osce.org/odihr/667164.body: Press release Dialogue and education are key to prevent violence based on religion or belief, OSCE human rights body says Date: 21 August 2026 Place: WARSAW Source: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights WARSAW, 21 August 2026 – Education about religions and beliefs, together with interfaith and interreligious dialogue, can help counter prejudice and hostility that can lead to violence, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) said in a statement ahead of tomorrow’s International Day Commemorating the Victims of Acts of Violence Based on Religion or Belief. “Across the OSCE region, individuals and communities continue to face violence on account of their religion or belief, and states have a duty to prevent and effectively respond to such violence,” said ODIHR Director Maria Telalian. “They can do this by creating the conditions for mutual respect and peaceful coexistence, including through education that instills respect for the human dignity of each person, strengthening resilience to polarizing narratives, and equipping people to recognize and respond to misinformation and disinformation.” “Dialogue across religious and belief boundaries can help make diversity a familiar part of everyday life, encouraging understanding instead of fear, and helping to prevent and counter prejudice,” she said. Year after year, ODIHR’s annual Hate Crime Report documents that individuals and communities are targeted on the basis of religion or belief across broad sectors of society and in a range of spaces, including online. Limited opportunities for people to meet and understand those they perceive as different can allow stereotypes and prejudice to take hold. In the absence of direct interaction, perceptions can, instead, be shaped by hearsay, prejudice, misinformation and disinformation that exploit and reinforce fears that can fuel hostility. Online platforms can further amplify the spread of divisive or misleading content. “Respect for human rights, including freedom of religion or belief, means recognizing that people have the right to hold and express different religious or non-religious convictions, including the belief that their own religion or worldview is true, while respecting the rights and dignity of those who believe differently,” the ODIHR Director said. Through their OSCE commitments, participating States have committed to promote interfaith and intercultural dialogue as a way to foster respect and mutual understanding, and to counter intolerance. They have also undertaken to address the root causes of intolerance and discrimination through education. ODIHR assists in this work by providing guidance on fostering dialogue, as well as practical tools, resources and capacity-building support on freedom of religion or belief and hate crimes for state officials and civil society actors. https://tntd.osce.org/news/transnational.body: Enhancing youth crime and drug use prevention through education on legality and awareness campaigns addressing threats of organized crime and corruption Project Update OSCE brings schools, police and prosecutors together to prevent youth crime in Kyrgyzstan Issued on: 30 July 2026 Issued by: Transnational Threats Department , Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities Fields of work: Policing Strengthening the ability of schools, law enforcement and prosecution services to identify and support vulnerable young people before they become involved in crime was the focus of a national OSCE training held from 28 to 30 July in Issyk-Kul, Kyrgyzstan. The event brought together 30 social pedagogues, juvenile police inspectors, prosecutors and representatives of state institutions from across the Kyrgyz Republic to enhance early intervention and multi-agency co-operation in preventing youth delinquency. Organized by the OSCE Secretariat's Transnational Threats Department and the Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities, the three-day training combined expert presentations, practical exercises, interdisciplinary group work and scenario-based simulations to strengthen participants’ capacity to recognize early warning signs of delinquent behaviour and develop co-ordinated responses. Participants explored individual, family and social risk factors associated with juvenile offending, as well as practical methods for identifying vulnerable youth in school settings and referring them to appropriate support services. Particular attention was given to strengthening communication and referral mechanisms among educational institutions, law enforcement and prosecution services to ensure timely and effective interventions. “Every young person who slips into delinquency is a missed opportunity for early intervention. As social pedagogues, we have a responsibility to recognize the warning signs before they become crises. This training has strengthened our ability to work hand in hand with police and prosecutors, so that vulnerable youth receive support when it can still change the course of their lives,” said Kasiyet Emilbaeva, Social Pedagogue at Toktogul Satylganov Issyk-Kul Regional Boarding School, Kyrgyzstan. The programme also addressed contemporary forms of juvenile delinquency, including youth violence, extortion and drug-related offences in educational settings. Through interdisciplinary case analysis and crisis simulation exercises, participants developed practical skills in joint decision-making, de-escalation techniques and multi-agency case management, while identifying opportunities to strengthen local prevention networks and institutional co-operation. The training was organized within the framework of the OSCE-wide extrabudgetary project “Enhancing youth crime and drug use prevention through education on legality and awareness campaigns addressing threats of organized crime and corruption”, funded by Germany, with additional support from Andorra, Finland, Italy, Norway, Poland and Thailand. https://www.osce.org/news/osce-secretari.body: In support of strengthening capacities of Ukrainian authorities in preventing and combating illicit trafficking in weapons, ammunition and explosives in all its aspects News Item OSCE provides server equipment to strengthen Ukraine’s border security and counter illicit weapons trafficking Issued on: 3 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Secretariat Extra-Budgetary Support Programme for Ukraine Fields of work: Arms control In August 2026, the OSCE provided the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine (SBGS) with server equipment to strengthen its criminal analysis and operative-search activities against illicit trafficking in firearms and other cross-border threats. The donated equipment will enhance the capacity of SBGS criminal analysis units to process, store and exchange information, ensuring more reliable and resilient operative-search measures in line with the law enforcement mandate of the agency. This assistance package builds directly on the OSCE’s earlier support to SBGS through the provision of specialized software and relevant training. “Criminal networks constantly adapt their methods, and our analytical capabilities must evolve for adequate response. The analytical software provided by the OSCE previously gave our specialists powerful tools, and the server infrastructure we are receiving now will allow us to use those tools more effectively and at a greater scale. Together, this support will amplify our ability to identify links, detect patterns, and anticipate criminal threats, helping us turn information into actionable intelligence and more effectively disrupt organized cross-border crime,” said a representative of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine during the handover event. The procurement and donation of the equipment were carried out under the OSCE extrabudgetary project “ In Support of Strengthening Capacities of Ukrainian Authorities in Preventing and Combating Illicit Trafficking in Weapons, Ammunition and Explosives in All Its Aspects ”, funded by the European Union, Finland, France, Germany, and Poland.

https://hcnm.osce.org/news/hcnm/667374.body: News News Item OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities Christophe Kamp on first official visit to Georgia Issued on: 7 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities Fields of work: Conflict prevention and resolution , Human rights , National minority issues , Tolerance and non-discrimination , Education , Gender equality , Women, peace and security , Youth OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities Christophe Kamp visited Georgia from 31 August to 4 September 2026. During his visit, Kamp travelled to the municipality of Marneuli and to the city of Batumi. He also joined a European Union Monitoring Mission in Georgia patrol on the Administrative Boundary Line. In Tbilisi, the High Commissioner met with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Affairs Minister Maka Botchorishvili, Education, Science and Youth Minister Givi Mikanadze, State Minister for Reconciliation and Civic Equality Tea Akhvlediani, Public Defender Levan Ioseliani, and members of the Government and the parliament. Kamp also engaged with representatives of the international community, minority representatives and civil society organizations. In Batumi and Marneuli, Kamp met with local and regional authorities, community leaders, as well as teachers and directors of minority-language schools. He also had the opportunity to exchange with members of minority-led civil society organizations working to foster inter-community dialogue and strengthen the effective participation of national minorities in public life. His interlocutors underlined the important contribution of mother tongue-based multilingual education (MLE) in facilitating opportunities for persons belonging to national minorities while also helping to preserve communities' identities. They also discussed ways in which this contribution could be further recognized and supported. The High Commissioner noted that his office had supported the development of mother-tongue based MLE in Georgia at policy and implementation level for more than two decades. During his visit, the High Commissioner also exchanged views on the legal and institutional framework supporting the integration of Georgia's diverse society. In his meetings, Kamp discussed the importance of meaningful consultation of communities at all levels of government, as well as the effective participation of national minorities in political and public life. He also discussed the situation of conflict-affected populations. The visit was an opportunity for the High Commissioner to exchange with a broad range of stakeholders on social cohesion and inter-community relationships in Georgia, based on the office’s previous long-term engagement in the country. https://bih.osce.org/news/mission-bosnia.body: News News Item OSCE calls for safeguarding BHRT’s independence and functioning ahead of elections Issued on: 6 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina Fields of work: Media freedom and development SARAJEVO, 06 September 2026 - The OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina (Mission) calls on all relevant authorities to respect and implement binding court decisions, safeguard judicial independence and ensure the functioning and independence of BHRT ahead of the elections. Public service broadcasters play a particularly important role during elections by providing citizens with reliable information needed to make informed decisions. Beyond the immediate measures needed to ensure BHRT’s continued functioning, a sustainable long-term framework for public service broadcasting is necessary, with strong safeguards for its independence. The Mission also calls on all public officials, candidates and political parties to respect media freedom and provide an enabling environment for journalists to work freely and independently during the election period. News News Item Electoral Integrity and Public Confidence at the Heart of the 2026 General Elections Issued on: 3 September 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina Fields of work: Elections SARAJEVO, 3 September 2026 – With Bosnia and Herzegovina’s 2026 General Elections approaching, the OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina and Civil Society BiH today brought together election officials, civil society, media, academia and international partners to discuss new election technologies, electoral integrity and the importance of a peaceful and democratic election campaign. The conference , “What Can We Expect from the 2026 Elections? New Electoral Technologies, Election Integrity, and a Democratic Election Campaign,” takes place one day before the official campaign begins and one month ahead of Election Day on 4 October. For the first time, the General Elections will involve biometric voter identification and authentication, as well as ballot scanners and electronic transmission of election results. The Mission has worked closely with the Central Election Commission of Bosnia and Herzegovina (CEC BiH) in supporting preparations for the introduction of these technologies, alongside its broader support for electoral integrity and voter education. “These new technologies will make the electoral process more accurate, transparent and efficient, but it is not just technology alone that builds public confidence in election results,” said Ambassador Rick Holtzapple, Head of the OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina. “Confidence also depends on how elections are administered, observed, reported and explained to voters. All those involved, institutions, political parties, observers, civil society and the media, have a responsibility to contribute to an electoral process that citizens can trust.” "Despite strong support from international organizations and individual global powers for electoral integrity, democratic campaigning, and the building of a democratic society, and, to a certain extent, the introduction of new technologies, the responsibility for the integrity of the electoral process lies primarily with the politicians. They must demonstrate whether they are all finally committed to progress, democracy, and the European path, or if some still wish to continue with the undemocratic and corrupt practices of the past," said Laura Bošnjak, Project Manager of Civil Society BiH. "It is the citizens who elect them; therefore, those citizens must recognize serious platforms, turn out to vote in the largest possible numbers, and decide to whom they will entrust their future and what that future will look like. Participants also discussed the responsibility of political parties to conduct a peaceful, constructive and substantive campaign focused on issues affecting citizens, rather than divisive rhetoric and narratives that heighten ethno-national tensions. Particular attention was given to the participation of first-time voters and to the importance of accurate voter information about the new voting procedures. The OSCE Mission to BiH and Civil Society BiH call on all eligible citizens to exercise their right to vote on 4 October 2026, to seek information from reliable sources and to reject divisive rhetoric and misinformation. They also call on political parties and candidates to offer voters a peaceful, issue-based campaign focused on concrete solutions and the future of all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. https://oceea.osce.org/news/oceea/665011.body: Women, Water Management and Conflict Prevention — Phase III Project Update OSCE Supports Sustainable Water Management and Regional Co-operation at the 4th High-Level International Conference on the International Decade for Action “Water for Sustainable Development” (2018–2028) Issued on: 1 June 2026 Issued by: Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities From 25 to 28 May 2026, the OSCE actively participated in the Fourth High-Level International Conference on the International Decade for Action “Water for Sustainable Development”, 2018–2028, held within the framework of the Dushanbe Water Process, as part of preparations for its contribution to the 2026 UN Water Conference. Through its participation in several official sessions, the OSCE contributed to discussions on how countries can strengthen co-operation under increasing climate stress, while reinforcing the importance of linking policy dialogue with the lived realities of communities that depend on shared water resources. Water insecurity, compounded by the impacts of climate change and unequal access to resources, continues to affect communities across the OSCE region, particularly in shared river basins where co-operation is essential for sustainable water management and resilience. Ahead of the Conference, the Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities (OCEEA) organized a three-day regional workshop, “Promoting Collaboration over Shared Water: Concepts and Approaches for Building Trust and Co-operation” in partnership with the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH) and with support from the Regional Environmental Centre for Central Asia. The regional workshop brought together women water professionals and young experts from across Central Asia to develop practical recommendations for strengthening co-operation focused on stronger data sharing, more effective communication, and more inclusive decision-making in transboundary water management. These recommendations were presented during a reception marking UNU-INWEH’s 30th anniversary, highlighting the work of the Women in Water Diplomacy Network. The discussions underscored a shared message: sustainable water security depends on inclusive participation and shared responsibility. During the Conference itself, the OSCE contributed to multiple sessions, including the opening plenary and several policy dialogues. On 25 May, it co-hosted the Youth Water Forum with the Government of Tajikistan, represented by the Ministry of Energy and Water Resources of the Republic of Tajikistan. Young participants called for stronger and more meaningful involvement in global water decision-making, and their outcome statement will help inform future policy processes. The same day, the OSCE contributed to the Women Water Forum, which underscored the importance of co-operation on water and glaciers and reinforced the value of inclusive approaches to shared environmental challenges. Together, these engagements demonstrated that water diplomacy is ultimately about people—building trust and fostering more secure and resilient societies. At the interactive dialogue on “Water for People,” Bakyt Dzhusupov, Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities**,** delivered an “ignite speech” emphasizing the foundations of effective water co-operation and noted: “Water co-operation across borders depends on transparency, dialogue, trust, and strong institutions that can manage shared resources peacefully. Climate change is intensifying these challenges, with droughts, floods, and shifting rainfall patterns exposing and deepening existing vulnerabilities, especially in fragile contexts. This reinforces that water governance is not only a development issue, but also a matter of peace and stability. Building resilient societies requires more than technical solutions alone.” The Conference served as an important platform for strengthening partnerships, mobilizing collective action, and advancing the implementation of the UN Water Action Agenda and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, while providing an opportunity to reflect on priorities for the post-2030 framework. These activities were implemented under the OSCE extra-budgetary project “ Women, Water Management and Conflict Prevention – Phase III ,” funded by Germany, Liechtenstein, Switzerland, and Finland. https://www.osce.org/chairpersonship/667.body: Press release OSCE Economic and Environmental Forum focuses on anticipating technologies and science diplomacy for emerging security risks Date: 10 September 2026 Place: PRAGUE Source: OSCE Chairpersonship , OSCE Secretariat PRAGUE, 10 September 2026 – The OSCE today opened its 32nd Economic and Environmental Forum (EEF) in Prague, focusing on how anticipating technological developments and strengthening science-based diplomacy can contribute to security and stability across the OSCE area by helping participating States better prepare for both existing and emerging challenges. Organized by the Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities under the guidance of Switzerland’s 2026 OSCE Chairpersonship, the two-day conference brings together representatives of OSCE participating States, Partners for Co-operation, international organizations, academia, the private sector and civil society. Participants are examining how the OSCE can strengthen its ability to anticipate technological developments, assess their implications for security and stability, and better prepare for a rapidly changing economic and environmental landscape. The discussion follows a Joint Preparatory Meeting of the EEF in Vienna from 7 and 8 September under the same title. In his address to the EEF participants, OSCE Chairman-in-Office, Swiss Federal Councillor Ignazio Cassis, recalled that “Anticipation is a political necessity. This is why Switzerland has chosen Anticipating technologies as a priority of its Chairpersonship. We must anchor this approach in the OSCE, because technology already affects all three dimensions of the OSCE.” As host of the event, which is taking place at Czernin Palace, Czech Deputy Prime Minister Petr Macinka, opened the EEF: “We must prepare the OSCE for the security challenges of tomorrow,” Minister Macinka said in his opening remarks. He stressed that new technologies, including artificial intelligence and quantum technologies, can become major sources of prosperity, innovation and resilience, while also creating new risks and changing the nature of security threats. “If we want to prevent conflicts and misunderstandings, we need to understand the impact of technological change before it catches us by surprise. This is precisely where the OSCE can play an important role,” the Czech Foreign Minister added. “Today, as geopolitical fragmentation is growing, we are also at the dawn of a new technological revolution. The direction this transformation takes will depend on the choices we make – collectively, as governments, as societies and as the international community. No single country, company, or institution can make those choices alone. This is why we need dialogue, co-operation and science-based diplomacy. And this is why our ability to anticipate matters so much,” said OSCE Secretary General Feridun H. Sinirlioğlu. During the opening session, the State Secretary of the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, Alexandre Fasel, stated that “The OSCE was founded on a comprehensive approach to security. This common ground endures despite our current divisions: the fact that we were able to agree to hold this Forum is a clear demonstration of this.” The Forum offers concrete follow-up to one of Switzerland’s priorities for its 2026 Chairpersonship: “anticipating technologies – for a safe and humane future”. It builds in particular on the international conference hosted in Geneva on 7and 8 May, which brought together experts from science, technology, diplomacy and policymaking to examine how anticipation can help societies prepare for rapid technological change. In Prague, participants are discussing how the OSCE can make better use of technological and scientific expertise in decision-making, strengthen anticipatory capacities and preparedness, and develop effective approaches to new technologies, including in relation to economic and environmental issues, in particular water, energy and economic good governance. The focus of this mandated, second dimension conference is part of the Swiss Chairpersonship’s broader effort to strengthen the OSCE’s ability to act in a changing security environment. For more information about this year’s event, click here . https://www.fidh.org/en/en/region/Africa.body: 12/08/2026 Statement Chad en es fr International Criminal Court (ICC) JORIS BOLOMEY / AFP The announcement by Chadian authorities of their decision to withdraw from the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC) marks a worrying setback for the fight against impunity for the most serious crimes and for victims’ rights. Chad’s commitment to international justice is called into question at a time when the international justice system is facing growing attacks and when state cooperation is more essential than ever. N’Djamena, 12 August 2026. On 27 July 2026, the Government of the Republic of Chad decided to withdraw from the Rome Statute of the ICC. The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), the Chadian League for Human Rights (LTDH), the Chadian Association for the Promotion and Defense of Human Rights (ATPDH), and the Public Interest Law Center (PILC) express their profound indignation and condemn this decision. The Rome Statute does not replace national courts; it operates on the basis of complementarity, stepping in when national courts lack the capacity or willingness to investigate and prosecute the most serious crimes. Withdrawal does not strengthen the ability of national courts to deliver justice; instead, it deprives victims of an alternative path to obtaining it. Chad’s withdrawal represents a further setback for the global fight against impunity and for victims’ rights, at a time when the Court is facing unprecedented attacks, including the U.S. government’s campaign to dismantle the ICC . Chad’s announcement does not, however, carry immediate legal consequences. Article 127 of the Rome Statute governs the effects of such a withdrawal: it takes effect only one year after written notification to the UN Secretary-General , in this case, on 27 July 2027. Moreover, withdrawal does not release the State concerned from obligations incurred while it was a party to the Statute, including the obligation to cooperate with the Court on investigations and criminal proceedings already underway before the withdrawal takes effect, and it does not affect investigations or proceedings the Court had already opened before that date. Chad’s withdrawal, should it go forward, therefore cannot erase the past or prevent the Court from exercising jurisdiction over crimes committed before it takes effect. Chad’s announcement comes amid a growing challenge to international criminal justice and the ICC. The three member States of the Alliance of Sahel States (Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger) also recently announced their withdrawal from the ICC. Those withdrawals will take effect on 18 June 2027 for Niger, and 24 June 2027 for Burkina Faso and Mali. African States nonetheless played an essential role in the creation of the Court in 1998, ratifying the Rome Statute in large numbers and even referring certain domestic situations to the Court’s jurisdiction. That commitment gave victims of the most serious crimes an international ally when justice could not be obtained at the national level. Chad’s announced withdrawal runs counter to this history of African leadership, leaving victims with fewer means of obtaining justice. While the ICC has in the past been criticised for the selectivity of the cases it opens and for what was seen as excessive focus on Africa, the Court has progressively worked to strengthen the universality of its mandate, extending its work well beyond the African continent, with ongoing investigations and cases in Afghanistan, Bangladesh/Myanmar, Palestine, Ukraine, Venezuela, and the Philippines. The recent arrest of former President Rodrigo Duterte demonstrated that no region and no senior official is beyond the reach of justice. This universality strengthens the Court’s legitimacy but also makes it more vulnerable to political attacks. The organisations call on Chadian authorities to reverse their decision to withdraw from the ICC and to reaffirm their commitment to the Rome Statute and to international justice. As Chad hosts several hundred thousand refugees from Darfur, many of whom have suffered serious violations of international humanitarian and human rights law, this announcement sends an alarming signal to victims. Victims of the most serious international crimes must not be the first casualties of States’ political choices. When national courts are unable or unwilling to deliver justice, the ICC remains an essential mechanism of last resort to guarantee victims’ right to truth, justice, and reparation. At a time when serious human rights violations persist in many parts of the world, States should be strengthening international mechanisms against impunity, not distancing themselves from them. FIDH, LTDH, ATPDH, and PILC reaffirm their determination to continue, alongside the whole of Chadian and international civil society, the fight against impunity and for justice, victims’ dignity, and respect for human rights in Chad. https://www.fidh.org/en/en/region/asia/i.body: 28/08/2026 Statement India en fr United Nations FIDH The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) welcomes the findings and recommendations made by the United Nations (UN) Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) related to India. FIDH urges the Indian authorities to fully implement the CERD’s recommendations without delay, particularly regarding comprehensively criminalising discrimination and hate crimes, and ensuring accountability for perpetrators of related human rights violations. Paris, 28 August 2026 . On 25 August 2026, the UN CERD released its findings and recommendations (known as " Concluding Observations ") concerning India, following the review of the country’s combined 20th and 21st periodic reports on the implementation of the International Convention on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (ICERD), which took place on 11 and 12 August 2026 in Geneva. The CERD monitors the implementation of the ICERD’s provisions by state parties, including India. Some of the CERD’s Concluding Observations reflected information presented by FIDH and partners in two joint reports submitted to the CERD as part of its review of India. For example, the CERD expressed concern over gaps in the Indian legislative framework, including the lack of a comprehensive definition of racial discrimination and the failure to explicitly criminalise all acts of racist hate speech and hate crimes. It also expressed concerns about " reports of widespread racial discrimination, including hate crimes and hate speech " including by politicians. The CERD called on the Indian government to review the legislative framework to address these gaps, and to take effective measures to increase accountability for hate speech and hate crimes. The CERD was " gravely concerned " by reports of widespread human rights violations against ethnic and ethno-religious groups, Indigenous and Tribal Peoples, and non-citizens, including extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detentions, torture, and sexual violence. It called on the Indian authorities to ensure that perpetrators are prosecuted and held accountable. With regards to civic space, the CERD raised concerns over the use of laws such as the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA), the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act (AFSPA) and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) to stifle the rights to freedom of expression and association, and to silence human rights defenders, including those working to defend the rights of minorities. It recommended that the authorities review those laws and ensure an enabling environment for civil society. The CERD also expressed concerns about, and made recommendations to address, the specific situations for Dalits, Indigenous and Tribal Peoples, nomadic and semi-nomadic tribes, domestic workers, and migrants and asylum seekers. The CERD noted in particular its concerns relating to the deportation and forcible returns of Rohingya asylum seekers, as well as the use of hate speech by politicians and other public figures targeting Rohingya and Bengali-speaking Muslims. Finally, the CERD made recommendations related to the right of freedom of thought, conscience and religion, the right to health, and the National Register of Citizens and Citizenship Amendment Act. https://www.fidh.org/en/en/region/americ.body: 10/09/2026 Report Ecuador en es fr Human Rights Defenders Antonella Calle International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and six international organisations denounce the climate of repression and militarisation in Ecuador. A new report, prepared following a visit to Ecuador, includes on-the-ground interviews with various communities, human rights defenders, local authorities, and representatives of the international community. Quito, September 10, 2026. Following an observation visit conducted in March 2026, the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), within the framework of the Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, Front Line Defenders (FLD), CIVICUS: Global Alliance for Citizen Participation, 11.11.11 – Coalition for International Solidarity, the Association of Human Rights Lawyers, Judges, and Prosecutors of Latin America and the Caribbean (Asociación de Abogadas, Abogados, Jueces y Fiscales de Derechos Humanos de América Latina y el Caribe – AJUFIDH), Peace Brigades International (PBI), and the World Rainforest Movement (WRM) are publishing a joint report today that warns of the rapid deterioration of the human rights and environmental situation in Ecuador. Against a backdrop marked by the militarisation of public security, the weakening of the rule of law, and a growing link between extractive conflicts and the securitisation of territories, the report, in spanish only, " Ataques y criminalización contra la sociedad civil en un contexto de militarización y extractivismo en Ecuador " presents the following findings. Setback in the Rule of Law Since March 2024, the government has repeatedly imposed states of emergency, declared internal armed conflict, and expanded the role of the Armed Forces in public safety, thereby normalising exceptional measures that have failed to reduce public insecurity in the country. On the contrary, the number of violent deaths has reached historic highs, and serious human rights violations are being reported in militarized areas, with disproportionate impacts on Indigenous peoples, Afrodescendant communities, and rural campesino communities. " Ecuador stands at a crossroads: either it strengthens the rule of law or it deepens the crisis. Exceptional measures cannot become the new normal, and socioenvironmental conflicts cannot be resolved through the militarisation of territories. A security policy in the country must address the multidimensional causes of violence and must adhere to international law, " states Soraya Gutierrez, Secretary General of the FIDH. Institutional Weakening The organisations note attacks on the Constitutional Court, challenges to judicial independence, delays in the administration of justice, and in the enforcement of court rulings, as well as an insufficient response from the Defensoría del Pueblo (Ombudsman’s Office / People’s Advocate Office) to the criminalisation and freezing of bank accounts of human rights defenders and civil society organisations. In this regard, César Sivo, president of AJUFIDH , states that " judicial independence is non-negotiable: without autonomous powers, the rule of law vanishes and justice becomes a mirage ". Criminalisation of Protest and Shrinking of Civic Space The report identifies patterns of violent repression against peaceful protests led by Indigenous movements, including criminalisation, stigmatisation, and the persecutory use of administrative, financial, and legal measures against human rights defenders and civil society organisations. " We observed a concerning and accelerating deterioration of civic space. The violent repression of the 2025 national strike, coupled with the increase in threats and attacks against journalists, as well as regulatory obstacles to the operation of civil society organisations, create an increasingly hostile environment for the exercise of civic freedoms, " emphasised Eduardo Marenco, Advocacy Officer for the Americas at CIVICUS. Attacks on Human Rights and Environmental Defenders, Civil Society Organisations and Social Movements The visit documents an alarming rate of violence and attacks against human rights and environmental defenders and civil society organisations, with particular attention to cases of criminalization, while the State fails to acknowledge the scale of this problem and adopt robust and effective measures to prevent these violations and protect defenders. " Defending human rights and nature is not a crime, as Ecuador’s own Constitution recognises. The criminalisation, stigmatisation, and attacks against defenders in Ecuador must cease immediately. The State has an obligation to protect those who defend the rights of their communities, not to persecute them, " says Álvaro Gómez del Valle, Advocacy Lead for the Americas at Front Line Defenders. The Rise of Extractivism Far from being a mere sectoral economic policy, extractivism—which spans the mining, oil, agro-industrial, fishing, and hydroelectric sectors—emerges as a web of regulatory, institutional, and security decisions that favor its expansion in the name of economic growth and investment stability in the country. This dynamic occurs at the expense of guarantees of participation, protection of rights, and compliance with democratic and judicial decisions, without respecting Ecuador’s international human rights obligations, which ultimately affect community governance, livelihoods, and the ability of communities to make free and informed decisions regarding their own territories. Regarding this serious issue, Carla Moscoso, Coordinator for the Andean Region of 11.11.11 , notes that " What is at stake is who decides on the territories, which ways of life are protected, and who bears the social and environmental costs of the conflicts, in the face of certain perspectives or categories such as ‘national interest,’ ‘strategic security,’ or ‘strategic sectors’ ." Among their urgent recommendations, the organisations urge the Ecuadorian government to: – align security policies with the principles of legality, necessity, and proportionality, with civilian and judicial oversight over the use of force; – guarantee the independence of public authorities; – put an end to the stigmatisation and criminalisation of protesters, individuals, and organisations defending human and nature rights; – protect human rights and nature defenders and groups through comprehensive policies that incorporate a gender and intercultural perspective; – respect the free, prior, and informed consent of communities affected by extractive projects. At the same time, the organisations call on the international community to: – not normalise the erosion of human rights as a cost of security policies and economic development initiatives; – strengthen monitoring and support for human rights defenders and civil society organisations. " The international community cannot look the other way. Ecuador needs strong support to protect those who defend rights. Our organisations will remain vigilant through international oversight and will closely monitor the human rights situation in the country ," emphasised the signatory organisations. https://www.fidh.org/en/en/region/Africa.body: 31/08/2026 Press release Democratic Republic of Congo en es fr Belgium Corruption NICOLAS MAETERLINCK / BELGA MAG / BELGA VIA AFP For the first time, a Belgian company will have to answer in court over allegations that it bribed foreign public officials. Congolese citizens, supported by a coalition of organisations, have joined the proceedings as civil parties before the Belgian courts. Part of the money paid for passports has allegedly been channelled to a relative of former Congolese President Joseph Kabila. The civil parties hope that justice will now be served in this case, which has been ongoing for nine years, and concerns the alleged embezzlement of US$60 million. Kinshasa, Brussels, 31 August 2026. The civil parties welcome the decision handed down this morning by the Brussels Council Chamber today to refer the 14 defendants in the Semlex case to the criminal court. They will have to answer allegations of bribery of foreign public officials, money laundering and tax fraud in connection with the contract for Congolese biometric passports. Semlex, the company that produced the Democratic Republic of Congo’s (DRC) biometric passports between 2015 and 2025, is the first Belgian company to be referred to a Belgian criminal court over alleged foreign bribery, with the prospect of the case being examined on its merits. In May 2020, 51 Congolese citizens brought a civil action before the Belgian courts with the support of the coalition Le Congo n’est pas à vendre (Congo Is Not For Sale). They were joined by the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), the Human Rights League (LDH), UNIS, Transparency International and Transparency International Belgium, all of which joined the proceedings as civil parties in this landmark case. The civil parties commend the work of the investigators who, over nearly nine years, traced bank transactions, analysed hundreds of emails and electronic messages, interviewed numerous witnesses and suspects, and carried out letters rogatory in the DRC and the United Arab Emirates, where several of the companies involved were registered. This is one of the most thorough investigations ever conducted in Belgium into allegations of international corruption. A US$60 million case The accused are alleged to have set up a large-scale corruption scheme centred on the biometric passport contract. According to documents reported in the press, for every passport sold for US$185, US$60 was allegedly channeled to LRPS Ltd, a Dubai-based company believed to be linked to a close associate of former DRC President Joseph Kabila. The scheme is alleged to have resulted in the diversion of nearly US$60 million. For the civil parties, this case concerns, above all, the Congolese people. " We paid $185 for our passports, before learning from the press that some of that money had allegedly been used to bribe members of the political elite. We have a right to know where our money went. This trial will finally shed light on the matter " said Fred Bauma, Congolese citizen acting as a civil claimant . " It is hoped that this case will also shed light on responsibilities at the Congolese level, which could lead to further legal action in the DRC, so that all those responsible in this case are held to account for their actions before the competent courts ", said Jean-Claude Katende, Vice-President of the FIDH and President of the African Association for the Defence of Human Rights (ASADHO) . This decision also marks a significant step forward for the Belgian justice system. Despite its commitments under the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention and the United Nations Convention against Corruption , the country has been criticised on several occasions for its inadequate enforcement of laws against the bribery of foreign public officials. This trial will be a major test of its ability to uphold these commitments. " For far too long, Belgium has fallen short of its commitments to combat international corruption. This referral to court is historic: it demonstrates that a Belgian company can be held to account for serious alleged acts of corruption committed abroad " said Transparency International Belgium . The signatory organisations stress that those brought before the court are presumed innocent. They hope that the trial will establish responsibility and send a clear message: Belgian companies must be held to account for their actions, including when alleged acts of corruption are committed abroad.
